title: Cinematography and Video Synthesis
answer: Text to video, virtual lensing, digital doubles, storyboarding and frame interpolation.

children.name: Text to Video, Physics and Continuity
children.blurb: Text to video covers systems that take a written prompt and produce a moving image sequence, and the craft question of whether that sequence holds together as a film would.

children.name: Virtual Camera and Lensing
children.blurb: Virtual camera and lensing covers the simulated camera inside a rendered or generated scene: its position, its movement, its focal length, its aperture, and the way light is bent through glass that may not exist.

children.name: Face Replacement and Digital Doubles
children.blurb: Face replacement and digital doubles cover the work of putting one performer's face onto another body, or building a synthetic performer that stands in for a real one across a shot, a scene or an entire production.

children.name: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
children.blurb: Storyboarding and pre-visualization cover the planning stage of a moving image project, where shots, camera moves, timing and staging are worked out before principal photography or full rendering begins.

children.name: Frame Interpolation and Restoration
children.blurb: Frame interpolation and restoration covers the work of repairing and smoothing moving images: removing dirt, scratches, noise and compression artefacts from old or damaged footage, and generating new frames between existing ones so that material shot at a low frame rate plays back smoothly.

sections.body: Cinematography and video synthesis covers systems that generate moving images from text prompts, sketches, or existing footage, and the tools that shape those images as a camera would. In practice, text to video models produce short clips from a written description, and the results are increasingly used for pitch reels, advertising tests, and background plates rather than finished feature work. Virtual lensing lets a director choose focal length, depth of field, and camera movement after a shot is generated, which shifts some decisions from the set to the edit. Digital doubles and face replacement are used in production for stunt work, de-aging, and continuity fixes, often in short inserts rather than whole performances. Frame interpolation and restoration fill gaps between frames or repair damaged footage, and both run quietly inside larger post pipelines.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is moving quickly but unevenly. Short clips of a few seconds can look convincing, while longer sequences drift in physics, lighting, and object identity, so continuity remains the central unsolved problem. Hands, reflections, and contact between objects still fail often enough that most professional use is confined to shots where errors can be hidden or fixed. Digital doubles work well for brief or distant appearances and less well for sustained close-ups where subtle facial motion matters. Restoration and interpolation are the most mature parts, though interpolation can introduce warping around fast motion and fine detail. Rights, consent, and credit for a performer's likeness are active questions in contracts and courts, not settled technical matters.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section is arranged from generation through control to repair. Text to Video, Physics and Continuity is the entry point, explaining what current models can produce and where they break down over time. Virtual Camera and Lensing follows, covering how focal length, framing, and movement are chosen or reconstructed after generation. Face Replacement and Digital Doubles deals with inserting and sustaining human likeness, including the consent and continuity issues that come with it. Storyboarding and Pre-visualization shows the earlier stage, where these tools serve planning rather than final output. Frame Interpolation and Restoration closes the section with the post production work of smoothing motion and recovering old or damaged material.
